passages.t: The earth laid waste, and the city of chaos
passages.happening:
‘Behold, the LORD lays waste the earth and leaves it in ruins’ (verse 1). He twists its surface and scatters its people, and no one is spared: people and priest, servant and master, maid and mistress, buyer and seller, lender and borrower (verse 2). The earth will be utterly laid waste, for the LORD has spoken (verse 3).

‘The earth mourns and withers; the world languishes and fades’ (verse 4). ‘The earth is defiled by its people; they have transgressed the laws; they have overstepped the decrees and broken the everlasting covenant’ (verse 5). So a curse consumes the earth, and only a few survive (verse 6).

The new wine dries up and the merrymakers groan. The tambourines and harps fall silent (verses 7-9). ‘The city of chaos is shattered; every house is closed to entry’ (verse 10). People cry out for wine in the streets, and joy is exiled from the land (verse 11). The city is left in ruins, its gate in rubble (verse 12). Among the nations it will be like an olive tree beaten bare, like the gleanings after the grape harvest (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Chapters 13 to 23 pronounced judgment on one nation after another. Chapter 24 lifts the view from the map to the globe. The word for earth or land runs through the chapter again and again, and no nation is named at all. It opens chapters 24 to 27, which gather the oracles against the nations into one picture of worldwide judgment followed by worldwide salvation.

These chapters are often called the Isaiah apocalypse, and when they were written is debated. The traditional view assigns them to Isaiah in the late eighth or early seventh century BC; some who hold it suggest that the fallen city could be Babylon, which Sennacherib destroyed in 689 BC. Many critical scholars date the section later. Bernhard Duhm put it as late as the second century BC; most since have placed it in the Persian period after the exile, because of its worldwide scope, its themes of cosmic judgment and resurrection, and its likeness to later apocalyptic writing. The Great Isaiah Scroll already contains these chapters.

The unnamed city of verses 10 to 12 has been identified with Babylon, Nineveh, Samaria, Jerusalem, Tyre and others. Many readers now think the anonymity is deliberate: the city stands for every proud human city organized without God.

The everlasting covenant broken in verse 5 is read by many as the covenant God made with Noah and every living creature, which bound all people to honor life. The first hearers would have heard that no one, priest or slave, rich or poor, stands outside God's judgment.
passages.later: The covenant with Noah is called ‘the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature’ (Genesis 9:16). Hosea says of his own land, ‘the land mourns, and all who dwell in it will waste away’ (Hosea 4:3).
passages.hard:
Is it just for God to lay waste the whole earth, including people who never heard of Israel's covenant?

The chapter itself raises the question by making the judgment universal. Its answer is that all humanity stands in a covenant relationship with God as Creator: the earth is defiled because its people have broken the laws and the everlasting covenant, which many interpreters read as the covenant with Noah. Paul makes a similar argument, that people without the written law still know enough of God and of right and wrong to be accountable (Romans 2:14-15).

The chapter is poetry of vision, gathering all human rebellion into one picture, and readers differ over how much it describes a single final event and how much the pattern of every judgment in history. And it does not delight in the destruction. Judgment in Isaiah is always followed by the offer of a feast for all peoples, which comes in the very next chapter.

This is not a key for reading any disaster today as God's judgment on those who suffer it.
passages.asks: No one in this chapter is exempt, not the priest, not the master, not the lender. Ask whether you think of yourself as outside God's judgment because of your position. And ask what the silence of the harps says about joy built without God.

passages.t: Songs from the ends of the earth, and the LORD reigns on Zion
passages.happening:
Voices are raised and shout for joy. From the west they proclaim the LORD's majesty (verse 14). In the east and in the islands of the sea, people glorify the name of the LORD, the God of Israel (verse 15). From the ends of the earth comes the song, ‘Glory to the Righteous One’ (verse 16).

But the prophet says he is wasting away, for the treacherous still betray (verse 16). ‘Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of the earth’ (verse 17). Whoever flees the sound of panic falls into the pit; whoever climbs out is caught in the snare. ‘For the windows of heaven are open, and the foundations of the earth are shaken’ (verse 18). The earth is broken apart and split open (verse 19). ‘The earth staggers like a drunkard and sways like a shack’ (verse 20).

‘In that day the LORD will punish the host of heaven above and the kings of the earth below’ (verse 21). They will be gathered like prisoners in a pit and punished after many days (verse 22). ‘The moon will be confounded and the sun will be ashamed; for the LORD of Hosts will reign on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem, and before His elders with great glory’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Songs of praise rise from the ends of the earth, but the prophet cannot join them yet. He sees treachery still at work, and he knows judgment is not finished. The same trap appears in Jeremiah's oracle on Moab, terror, pit and snare, three words that sound alike in Hebrew.

The windows of heaven opened recall the flood in Noah's day. The earth staggers like a drunk, and a hut in a field sways in the wind. The world as it is cannot stand.

The host of heaven in verse 21 is read by many as the spiritual powers behind the nations, judged together with the earthly kings who served them. The first hearers were told that every power, seen and unseen, answers to the LORD.

The chapter ends on the note the next three chapters develop. The sun and moon, worshiped by the nations, are ashamed beside the glory of the LORD, who reigns as king on Mount Zion. The feast of chapter 25, the songs of chapter 26 and the gathering of chapter 27 all flow from that final verse.
passages.later: Jeremiah turns the same words on Moab: ‘Terror and pit and snare await you, O dweller of Moab’ (Jeremiah 48:43). In Noah's flood ‘the floodgates of the heavens were opened’ (Genesis 7:11). And Revelation pictures the city that ‘has no need of sun or moon to shine on it, because the glory of God illuminates the city’ (Revelation 21:23).
passages.asks: The prophet could not sing yet, because he still saw treachery. Ask whether your joy is honest about the wrongs still in the world. And ask what it means for you that the LORD will reign on Zion when every other power has been brought low.
